pages.title: A steady week. A smaller next plan.

blocks.text: You saved seven hours across six study days. The important next move is to make your upcoming workload fit the time you actually have, while protecting preparation for Friday's Biology exam.

blocks.label: Keep
blocks.text: Keep the six-day rhythm if it suits you. Your recorded study days were close in length: 65-75 minutes. There is no need to make every day longer simply to make the chart look better.

blocks.label: Adjust
blocks.text: Allow more room for similar Maths tasks. Three completed, linked tasks took 135 minutes against 90 estimated minutes. Treat that as a planning signal for these tasks, not a judgement of your ability.

blocks.label: Prioritise
blocks.text: Protect 135 minutes of Biology preparation before the exam date. Your original next-week list needs 420 minutes, but your entered availability supports 300 minutes. Review what to defer before adding work.

pages.title: Give the next deadline enough room.

blocks.title: Subject time in the context of your next goal

blocks.text: Maths received 270 minutes (64.3%) and Biology 150 minutes (35.7%). This split is not automatically a problem: equal time is not a requirement. It matters now because your next dated exam is Biology on Friday 20 November, and three selected preparation tasks still need an estimated 135 minutes.

The draft on page 3 reserves those three tasks first, then keeps two Maths priorities. It does not claim Biology is a weak subject or that more hours will guarantee exam readiness. Review the priorities against what your teacher or course actually requires.

blocks.title: Why similar tasks may need a larger estimate

blocks.text: For these three tasks, an average 30-minute estimate corresponded to 45 recorded minutes. For the next comparable practice task, try an editable 40-50 minute estimate, or split the work into two smaller parts. Check what remains after the first part rather than automatically extending every session.

The sample contains only three completed tasks with both an original estimate and linked records. It excludes unfinished work and tasks with missing estimates. The recorded effort is lifetime effort through the cutoff, not a claim that all future Maths work takes 50% longer. The cause of the mismatch is unknown.

blocks.title: What fits before the next deadline

blocks.text: The proposed plan schedules 255 study minutes and leaves 45 minutes unallocated for work that runs over. That means deferring 165 minutes, rather than only the bare 120-minute gap. The exam time was not entered, so Biology preparation is placed before the exam date; no exam-day preparation time is assumed.
Basis: E04 subject totals; E05 three matched task estimates; E06 next-week availability, breaks, task remaining-time estimates and exam date. Remaining time is user-estimated, not predicted by AI.

pages.title: Five priorities. Forty-five minutes of room.

blocks.text: This draft schedules 255 study minutes plus 45 minutes of buffer. It does not automatically change the previous 480-minute weekly target: review that target against this smaller commitment. Confirm the deadline, remaining-work estimates and availability before saving.

For each 45-minute Biology block, use 18:00-18:45; the entered 10-minute break leaves 15 minutes as unscheduled room. Each 60-minute Maths allocation is split into 18:00-18:30 and 18:40-19:10, with a 10-minute break. Saturday and Sunday remain unscheduled because no availability was entered.

blocks.label: If work runs over
blocks.text: Use the available buffer first. If Biology still has unfinished preparation after Wednesday, review Thursday's Maths allocation before adding time you have not entered. The report cannot know whether your remaining-time estimate covers everything needed for the exam.

blocks.label: When you accept
blocks.text: Review the draft in place, then explicitly save the selected changes. The draft is not a commitment until you accept it. Keep any existing commitments you cannot move; review a fresh draft if your free time changes.

pages.title: Make the next review easier to act on.

blocks.text: Across the four recorded weeks, saved study rose from 4 to 5 to 7 hours, then stayed at 7 hours. The latest week is a plateau in recorded time, not evidence of stalled understanding. Use completion and estimate accuracy alongside the time chart rather than chasing a longer bar.

blocks.text: All figures, task references, task names, exam details and action history in this example are fictional. This is an AI-written format demonstration, not an analysis of your account or a live DeepSeek result. A real report should identify its saved week, cutoff and missing information just as clearly.

Unrecorded study is not included. The 6/8 completion figure follows the original task baseline; the timing comparison covers only the three matched completed tasks. Next-week remaining-time values are your estimates. Check them if a task still seems too large.

Saved time and self-marked completion do not establish grades, attention or mastery. A report can help you review a plan; it cannot tell whether the task list covers everything you need for an exam. Your private reflections remain separate from the generated analysis.

blocks.label: Before your next review
blocks.text: After each priority session, check what remains and confirm completion when finished. At the next review, compare the linked tasks and their estimates with the plan you actually accepted. Keep the same saved report online or download it; the copy does not contain extra analysis.
